records.name: data/assembly/assembly-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/assembly/assembly-spec.md#Overview -->
## Overview

MOS 6510 (C64 CPU) is a NMOS 6502 core with an 8‑bit data path and a 16‑bit address space (64 KiB). Registers: `A`, `X`, `Y` (8‑bit), `PC` (16‑bit), `SP` (8‑bit, stack at `$0100..$01FF`), `P` status `[N V - B D I Z C]`. The stack grows downward; pushes write to `$0100+SP` then decrement `SP`.

records.name: data/assembly/assembly-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/assembly/assembly-spec.md#Lexical Conventions -->
## Lexical Conventions

- **Numbers:** decimal `42`, hexadecimal `$2A`, binary `%00101010`. Immediate prefix `#`.
- **Identifiers:** `[A–Z_][A–Z0–9_]*` (case‑insensitive).  
- **Labels:** an identifier followed by `:` defines the current address. Reference with the bare identifier (optionally signed offsets in expressions).
- **Comments:** `;` to end of line. Whitespace is insignificant except as separator.
- **Expressions:** integers with `+ - * / & | ^ ~ << >>` and parentheses (assembler‑dependent), may refer to labels and the current location counter `*`.

records.name: data/assembly/assembly-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/assembly/assembly-spec.md#Labels and Symbol Rules -->
## Labels and Symbol Rules

- **Definition:** `label:` binds `label` to the current address (`*`). Multiple labels may precede an instruction.
- **Use:** Any place an absolute/relative/address expression is expected (`LDA label`, `BEQ loop`).
- **Forward refs:** allowed; assembler resolves in a second pass.
- **Constants:** `name = expr` or `.equ name, expr` (assembler‑specific). Location counter may be set with `.org expr`. Data directives: `.byte`, `.word`, `.fill`, `.align` (names may vary).

records.name: data/assembly/assembly-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/assembly/assembly-spec.md#Instruction Semantics (brief) -->
## Instruction Semantics (brief)

- **Load/Store:** `LDA/LDX/LDY` load; `STA/STX/STY` store. Affect `N,Z` (stores don’t).
- **ALU:** `ADC/SBC` (use `CLC`/`SEC` before add/sub), `AND/ORA/EOR`, `INC/DEC` (memory), `INX/INY/DEX/DEY` (registers). Flags as per 6502.
- **Shifts/Rotates:** `ASL/LSR/ROL/ROR` on `A` or memory. Shifted‑out bit enters `C`.
- **Compare:** `CMP/CPX/CPY` set `C` for ≥, `Z` for =, `N` for sign of result (no writeback).
- **Branch:** `BPL/BMI/BVC/BVS/BCC/BCS/BNE/BEQ` use signed 8‑bit `REL` offset (−128..+127 from `PC+2`). Taken branch +1 cycle; +1 more if page crosses.
- **Jumps/Calls:** `JMP` `ABS|IND`, `JSR ABS`, `RTS`, `BRK`/`RTI`.
- **Stack/Flags/Xfer:** `PHA/PLA`, `PHP/PLP`, `TAX/TAY/TXA/TYA`, `TSX/TXS`, `CLC/SEC/CLI/SEI/CLD/SED/CLV`, `NOP`.
- **Decimal mode:** C64 typically keeps `D=0` (`CLD`). Use BCD only if intentional.

records.name: data/assembly/assembly-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/assembly/assembly-spec.md#EBNF (assembly source) -->
## EBNF (assembly source)

```ebnf
program     = { line } ;
line        = [ label ] , [ instruction | directive ] , [ comment ] , EOL ;
label       = identifier , ":" ;
instruction = mnemonic , [ operand ] ;
directive   = "." , ident , [ operandlist ] ;

operand     = expr
            | "#" , byte
            | "(" , expr , ")"                          (* IND for JMP *)
            | "(" , zp , "," , "X" , ")"                (* IZX *)
            | "(" , zp , ")" , "," , "Y"                (* IZY *)
            | expr , "," , "X"                          (* ABSX or ZPX *)
            | expr , "," , "Y"                          (* ABSY or ZPY *)
            ;
operandlist = expr , { "," , expr } ;

expr        = term , { ("+"|"-"|"|"|"^") , term } ;
term        = factor , { ("*"|"/"|"&") , factor } ;
factor      = ["+"|"-"|"~"] , primary ;
primary     = number | identifier | "(" , expr , ")" | "*" ;

mnemonic    = "ADC"|"AND"|"ASL"|"BCC"|"BCS"|"BEQ"|"BIT"|"BMI"|"BNE"|"BPL"|
              "BRK"|"BVC"|"BVS"|"CLC"|"CLD"|"CLI"|"CLV"|"CMP"|"CPX"|"CPY"|
              "DEC"|"DEX"|"DEY"|"EOR"|"INC"|"INX"|"INY"|"JMP"|"JSR"|"LDA"|
              "LDX"|"LDY"|"LSR"|"NOP"|"ORA"|"PHA"|"PHP"|"PLA"|"PLP"|"ROL"|
              "ROR"|"RTI"|"RTS"|"SBC"|"SEC"|"SED"|"SEI"|"STA"|"STX"|"STY"|
              "TAX"|"TAY"|"TSX"|"TXA"|"TXS"|"TYA" ;

identifier  = ( "A".."Z" | "_" ) , { "A".."Z" | "0".."9" | "_" } ;
number      = dec | "$" hex | "%" bin ;
dec         = "0".."9" , { "0".."9" } ;
hex         = hexDigit , { hexDigit } ;
bin         = "0"|"1" , { "0"|"1" } ;
hexDigit    = "0".."9" | "A".."F" ;
byte        = number ;      (* assembler validates range *)
zp          = number ;      (* assembler may restrict to 0..255 for ZP *)
comment     = ";" , { any-not-EOL } ;
EOL         = "\n" ;
```

---

### Addressing‑Mode Profiles (bytes/cycles)

Unless noted, page cross on `ABSX/ABSY/IZY` adds **+1** cycle.

| Group | Mode → bytes/cycles | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **ALU (ADC,AND,CMP,EOR,LDA,ORA,SBC)** | `#` 2/2 · `ZP` 2/3 · `ZPX` 2/4 · `ABS` 3/4 · `ABSX` 3/4+ · `ABSY` 3/4+ · `IZX` 2/6 · `IZY` 2/5+ | CMP shares counts; LDA as listed. |
| **STA** | `ZP` 2/3 · `ZPX` 2/4 · `ABS` 3/4 · `ABSX` 3/5 · `ABSY` 3/5 · `IZX` 2/6 · `IZY` 2/6 | Store does **not** set `N,Z`. |
| **STX** | `ZP` 2/3 · `ZPY` 2/4 · `ABS` 3/4 | |
| **STY** | `ZP` 2/3 · `ZPX` 2/4 · `ABS` 3/4 | |
| **LDX** | `#` 2/2 · `ZP` 2/3 · `ZPY` 2/4 · `ABS` 3/4 · `ABSY` 3/4+ | |
| **LDY** | `#` 2/2 · `ZP` 2/3 · `ZPX` 2/4 · `ABS` 3/4 · `ABSX` 3/4+ | |
| **INC/DEC (mem)** | `ZP` 2/5 · `ZPX` 2/6 · `ABS` 3/6 · `ABSX` 3/7 | |
| **INX/INY/DEX/DEY** | `IMP` 1/2 | |
| **ASL/LSR/ROL/ROR** | `A` 1/2 · `ZP` 2/5 · `ZPX` 2/6 · `ABS` 3/6 · `ABSX` 3/7 | |
| **BIT** | `ZP` 2/3 · `ABS` 3/4 | On 6510 only ZP/ABS. |
| **JMP** | `ABS` 3/3 · `IND` 3/5 | Buggy wrap on `IND`. |
| **JSR/RTS/RTI/BRK** | `JSR ABS` 3/6 · `RTS` 1/6 · `RTI` 1/6 · `BRK` 1/7 | |
| **Branches (Bcc)** | `REL` 2/2(+1 taken, +1 xpage) | |
| **Flag ops** | `IMP` 1/2 | `CLC,CLD,CLI,CLV,SEC,SED,SEI` |
| **Stack ops** | `PHA,PHP` 1/3 · `PLA,PLP` 1/4 | |
| **Transfers** | `TAX,TAY,TXA,TYA,TSX,TXS` 1/2 | |
| **NOP** | `IMP` 1/2 | Documented form only. |

<!-- Source: data/assembly/assembly-spec.md#Opcode Decode Table -->
### Opcode Decode Table

#### Scope

- Table order is strictly ascending by opcode from `00` to `FF`.
- `IMM` is the canonical mode token for **immediate** addressing.
- Elsewhere in the spec, immediate operands may be written with `#`, e.g. `LDA #$01`.
- `cycles` is the base cycle count.
- `page_cross_penalty` is only populated where an extra cycle can occur due to page crossing or branch flow.
- `KIL` does not complete normal execution; `cycles=halt`.

#### Semantic Conventions

- `M` = operand value after address resolution
- `[EA]` = memory at effective address
- `EA.hi` = high byte of effective address
- `push(x)` / `pop` / `pop16` = stack operations
- `set(...)` = update listed flags from result
- `ROL(x)` / `ROR(x)` = rotate through carry
- `rel` = signed relative branch displacement
- Unofficial unstable opcodes are marked explicitly with `unstable;`

#### Table Format

```text
opcode mnemonic mode flags cycles page_cross_penalty semantics
```

<!-- Source: data/assembly/assembly-spec.md#Minimal Directives (common) -->
### Minimal Directives (common)

- Location: `.org addr` / `* = addr`  
- Data: `.byte expr[,…]`, `.word expr[,…]`  
- Symbols: `name = expr` / `.equ name, expr`  
- Alignment/fill (assembler‑specific): `.align n`, `.fill count, value`
- Text: `.text "str"` / `.ascii "str"` convert ASCII to PETSCII for the default upper-case/graphics set: `a`-`z` and `A`-`Z` both become codes `$41`-`$5A`, `\n` becomes RETURN (`$0D`), other ASCII characters (digits, punctuation, space) are unchanged, and characters above `$7F` are an error.
- `.equ` accepts both `name .equ expr` and `.equ name, expr`; `.fill count[, value]` and `.align n[, fill]` default the fill byte to 0.

### Basic Start Header

- PRG file = 2-byte little-endian load address + bytes
- Place a tokenized BASIC line at $0801, e.g. `10 SYS 4096` (token SYS = $9E) to jump to $1000
- Ensure load-address at PRG start matches where BASIC was placed (e.g. $01 $08)
- Machine code may live at $1000 or directly after BASIC; adjust SYS target accordingly

# Commodore 64 BASIC V2 Specification

records.name: data/basic/basic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/basic/basic-spec.md#1. Overview -->
## 1. Overview

C64 BASIC V2 is a line-numbered, interpreted, tokenised language stored in ROM.  
Each program consists of linked line records beginning at `$0801`, and executes sequentially unless redirected by explicit control flow. The interpreter manages variables, arrays, and strings in RAM regions immediately following the program text.

---

records.name: data/basic/basic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/basic/basic-spec.md#2. Memory and Program Layout -->
## 2. Memory and Program Layout

records.name: data/basic/basic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/basic/basic-spec.md#2.2 BASIC Program Storage (PRG Format) -->
### 2.2 BASIC Program Storage (PRG Format)

Each BASIC program in memory (and on disk/tape) is a contiguous block:

| Field | Size | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| Load address | 2 bytes | `$0801` little-endian |
| Next line pointer | 2 bytes | Absolute address of next line |
| Line number | 2 bytes | 0–65535 |
| Tokenised PETSCII text | variable | Zero-terminated statement list |
| Terminator | 2 bytes | Final `$0000` sentinel |

Pointers increase monotonically. The final record’s pointer references the terminator.  
Tokenisation replaces keywords by single-byte codes (`$80–$CB`), ignoring quoted strings and `REM` comments. Empty lines are stored as a single `$20` (space).

---

records.name: data/basic/basic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/basic/basic-spec.md#3. Variables and Data Model -->
## 3. Variables and Data Model

records.name: data/basic/basic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/basic/basic-spec.md#3.2 Internal Representation -->
### 3.2 Internal Representation

| Offset | Field | Description |
|--------:|--------|-------------|
| 0–1 | Name (2 chars) with high bits as type markers | Identifier |
| 2–6 | Data payload | Depends on type |

**Encoding rules:**

- *Real*: ASCII name, 2nd byte zero if single char.  
- *Integer*: both name bytes have high-bit set.  
- *String*: only 2nd byte has high-bit set.

**Payload:**

- Real: exponent + mantissa (5 bytes).  
- Integer: 2-byte value, 3 bytes padding 0.  
- String: length (1 byte), pointer (2 bytes LE), padding 0s.

---

records.name: data/basic/basic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/basic/basic-spec.md#3.3 Arrays -->
### 3.3 Arrays

Declared via `DIM`, e.g. `DIM A(7)` (indices 0–7).  
If a program uses an array without prior `DIM`, BASIC auto-DIMs it to 11 elements per dimension (0–10).  
Re-DIMing → `?REDIM'D ARRAY ERROR`.  
Index < 0 or > 32767 → `?ILLEGAL QUANTITY ERROR`.

#### Internal Layout

```
name(2) , offset_to_next(2) , dimensions(1) ,
length1(2) [, length2(2)...] , data...
```

- Offset is relative to next array (for relocation).  
- `dimensions` = number of axes (1–255 theoretical).  
- Each element stored in ascending index order; leftmost index varies fastest.  
- Element sizes: Real 5 B, Integer 2 B, String 3 B descriptor.

**Examples:**

```
DIM C%(2,3)  → 3×4 = 12 integers
DIM S$(1,2,3) → 2×3×4 = 24 string descriptors
```

---

records.name: data/basic/basic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/basic/basic-spec.md#3.5 Variable Optimisation Guidelines -->
### 3.5 Variable Optimisation Guidelines

- Declare scalar variables before arrays (avoids array shifting).  
- Use short two-character names for speed.  
- Avoid redundant `LET`.  
- Keep string operations minimal in loops.  
- Use `FRE(0)` to inspect available memory (16-bit signed).  
- To locate start of variable table:

  ```
  VT = PEEK(46)*256 + PEEK(45)
  ```

---

records.name: data/basic/basic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/basic/basic-spec.md#4. Operators -->
## 4. Operators

| Rank | Operators | Description |
|------|------------|-------------|
| 1 | `^` | Exponentiation |
| 2 | unary `+ −` | Sign prefix |
| 3 | `* /` | Multiplication / Division |
| 4 | `+ −` | Addition, Subtraction, String concatenation |
| 5 | `< <= = >= > <>` | Comparison |
| 6 | `NOT` | Logical NOT / bitwise invert |
| 7 | `AND` | Logical AND / bitwise AND |
| 8 | `OR` | Logical OR / bitwise OR |

Parentheses nest ≤ 10 levels.  
Division by 0 → `?DIVISION BY ZERO`.  
Logical ops on integers act bitwise on 16-bit values.

---

## 9. Validation Rules

- Line numbers: 0–65535.  
- Each program ends with `$0000` sentinel.  
- Parentheses depth ≤10.  
- Array redefinition prohibited.  
- Division by zero → runtime error.  
- Out-of-memory or string overflow → `?OUT OF MEMORY`.  
- Keyword collision in variable name → `?SYNTAX ERROR`.

---

records.text:
<!-- Source: data/basic/basic-spec.md#10. Performance and Optimisation Guidelines -->
## 10. Performance and Optimisation Guidelines

C64 BASIC V2 is fully interpreted and float-based. Optimise by reducing parsing, conversions, and heap movement. Every line lookup and variable access incurs cost; fast programs minimise interpreter work.

records.name: data/basic/basic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/basic/basic-spec.md#10.1 Execution Model -->
### 10.1 Execution Model

- Each line is linked; `GOTO`, `GOSUB`, `IF` search from start. Keep hot loops in low line numbers.
- Keywords are tokenised; variables and literals parsed at runtime.
- Numeric work is float unless explicitly integer; type conversions are slow.

records.name: data/basic/basic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/basic/basic-spec.md#10.2 Variables -->
### 10.2 Variables

- Only first two name letters count—use short names.
- Define scalars before arrays; new scalars shift arrays by 7 B each.
- Floats faster than integers; mixed arithmetic incurs conversion.
- `FRE(0)` scans all variables—use sparingly.
- Use 0 and −1 for Boolean logic.

records.name: data/basic/basic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/basic/basic-spec.md#10.3 Arrays -->
### 10.3 Arrays

- Always `DIM`; undeclared arrays auto-DIM 11 elements per dimension.
- Re-DIM → error; index 0–32767 only.
- Keep dimensions small and fixed; leftmost index varies fastest.

records.name: data/basic/basic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/basic/basic-spec.md#10.4 Arithmetic -->
### 10.4 Arithmetic

- Replace `^` with multiplication; pre-compute constants and function results.
- `INT(X)` faster than truncation math; avoid mixing ints/floats.
- Keep loops tight; each iteration re-parses expressions.

records.name: data/basic/basic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/basic/basic-spec.md#10.5 Strings -->
### 10.5 Strings

- Heap grows downward, no garbage collection.
- Avoid `A$=A$+B$` in loops; prefer `PRINT A$;B$`.
- Reuse string vars; overwrite via `MID$` instead of reallocating.
- Use `CLR` to reclaim heap; `LEFT$/RIGHT$/MID$` create new descriptors—use sparingly.

records.name: data/basic/basic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/basic/basic-spec.md#10.6 Control Flow -->
### 10.6 Control Flow

- Prefer `FOR…NEXT` to manual `GOTO` loops.
- Keep `IF` expressions short; parser re-evaluates every branch.
- Combine short statements with `:` (< 80 chars per line).
- Limit nesting depth (< 5) for readability and speed.

records.name: data/basic/basic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/basic/basic-spec.md#10.8 Memory Use -->
### 10.8 Memory Use

- Each scalar = 7 B; arrays store only element data.
- Pack short related statements on one line.
- Use abbreviations (`?`, `gO`, `sT`) to stay within 80 chars.
- Maintain ≥ 50 % free RAM for string heap stability.
- Call `CLR` to drop unused variables.

records.name: data/basic/basic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/basic/basic-spec.md#10.9 Summary -->
### 10.9 Summary

Fast BASIC = minimal parsing, fixed data, short names, reused strings, few allocations.  
Define vars early, pre-DIM arrays, keep loops shallow, and avoid heap churn.  
Typical speed gain: 2–5× over unoptimised code.

---

records.name: data/basic/basic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/basic/basic-spec.md#11. Writing Games Efficiently in BASIC -->
## 11. Writing Games Efficiently in BASIC

C64 BASIC games rely on careful screen, input, and timing control. Interpreter speed limits frame rate; optimise for responsiveness, not raw throughput.
records.origin: data/basic/basic-spec.md#11. Writing Games Efficiently in BASIC

records.name: data/basic/basic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/basic/basic-spec.md#11.1 Core Strategy -->
### 11.1 Core Strategy

- BASIC handles logic; graphics/sound via `POKE` to hardware.
- Use fixed variables and arrays; avoid runtime string creation.
- Keep main loop short and predictable.

records.name: data/basic/basic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/basic/basic-spec.md#11.3 Delta Updates -->
### 11.3 Delta Updates

- Track old/new positions; erase previous cell, draw new one.
- Use flags or small arrays for active objects only.
- Skip unchanged elements; BASIC loops are costly.

records.name: data/basic/basic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/basic/basic-spec.md#11.10 Summary -->
### 11.10 Summary

Efficient BASIC games minimise interpreter overhead.  
Use `POKE/PEEK` for graphics and input, delta redraw for movement, fixed-step gating only when required, and pre-allocated variables for state.  
Result: smooth, responsive gameplay within BASIC’s limits.

<!-- Source: data/io/cia-spec.md#CIA #1 Registers (`$DC00–$DC0F`) — Keyboard/Joysticks/Paddles/Lightpen/IRQ -->
**Notes (CIA1):** Keyboard matrix via column write (PRA) + row read (PRB), active‑low. Joystick‑keyboard contention on **Port 1** (PRB) exists; avoid or gate scanning accordingly. Paddle select uses **PRA b7/b6**; paddle *positions* read via SID POTX/POTY; paddle buttons via CIA (bits 2–3). Lightpen appears as fire on PRA b4 and via VIC `/LP`.

records.name: data/io/cia-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/io/cia-spec.md#Time‑of‑Day (TOD) Clock — BCD + Alarm -->
## Time‑of‑Day (TOD) Clock — BCD + Alarm

- **Regs:** `$xx08–$xx0B` (10th, sec, min, hr). **Hours b7**=AM/PM.  
- **Write target:** **CRB7=0** write **time**; **CRB7=1** write **alarm**.  
- **Halt rule:** Writing **TODHR** halts update until **TOD10TH** is read (for read‑latch/write‑latch coherency).  
- **Tick source:** **CRA7** selects 60 Hz/50 Hz. **Alarm match** sets ICR bit2 (IRQ/NMI by CIA).

records.name: data/io/cia-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/io/cia-spec.md#Serial Shift (SDR) — SP/CNT -->
## Serial Shift (SDR) — SP/CNT

- **Direction:** **CRA6** (0=in, 1=out).  
- **Input:** On **CNT↑**, bit from **SP** shifts into SDR; byte complete → **ICR b3**.  
- **Output:** With Timer A running (cont.), SDR shifts MSB→LSB out **SP** with **CNT** strobes; byte complete → **ICR b3**.  
- **System:** OS uses port‑bit IEC more than SDR; SDR remains available on user port **SP1/CNT1** (CIA1) and **SP2/CNT2** (CIA2).

records.name: data/io/cia-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/io/cia-spec.md#Interrupts (ICR) — Mask/Status -->
## Interrupts (ICR) — Mask/Status

- **Status read (clears):** b0 TA UF, b1 TB UF, b2 TOD alarm, b3 serial, b4 FLAG; **b7**=any pending (ANDed with mask).  
- **Mask write:** **b7=1** sets bits 0–4; **b7=0** clears bits 0–4; bits written as 0 are unchanged.  
- **Wiring:** CIA1 ICR → **/IRQ**; CIA2 ICR → **/NMI** (not maskable by SEI).

- **Direct 6510 bus exposure:** A[15:0], D[7:0], R/W, Φ2, /IRQ, /NMI, /RESET, chip selects. Devices can map ROM/RAM/I/O and trap vectors. **No CIA mediation.**

<!-- Source: data/printer/printer-spec.md#Protocol Differences (critical) -->
## Protocol Differences (critical)

- **Character set:** MPS expects **PETSCII**; Epson expects **ASCII** with ESC/P sequences.  
- **Mode switching:** MPS uses single-byte PETSCII controls; Epson uses multi-byte ESC (27) commands.  
- **Graphics:** MPS Bit Image = 7-dot columns (bit7=1); Epson = 8-dot columns `(n,m)` pairs.  
- **Line endings:** Always send CR (13); often LF (10). FF (12) for page eject.

---

records.name: data/printer/printer-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/printer/printer-spec.md#Commodore MPS Essentials (Text) -->
## Commodore MPS Essentials (Text)

- **Open:** `OPEN ch,4[,sa]` (`sa=0` upper/graphics, `7` lower/upper).  
- **Print:** `PRINT#ch,…` or `CMD ch`.  
- **Close:** `CLOSE ch`.  
- **Bit Image:** Enter `CHR$(8)`; repeat `CHR$(26);count;byte`; exit `CHR$(15)`.

---

records.text:

## Epson FX Essentials (Text)

- **Pitch:** `ESC M` (12 cpi), `ESC P` (10 cpi). **Bold:** `ESC E`/`ESC F`.  
- **Underline:** `ESC - n`. **Spacing:** `ESC A n`. **Reset:** `ESC @`.

---

- **MPS:** 7 dots/byte; bit7=1; ≈60×72 dpi; max ~480 dots/line.  
- **Epson:** 8 dots/byte; multiple densities via `ESC K/L/Y/Z/*/^`; use `ESC A 8` for 8-dot rows.

<!-- Source: data/sound/sid-file-structure.md#Practical playback flow -->
## Practical playback flow

1) Read header (verify `PSID`/`RSID`).
2) Resolve `dataOffset` and `loadAddress`; if `loadAddress=0`, fetch it from first two data bytes.
3) Load data to RAM and call `initAddress` (or `loadAddress` if `initAddress=0`), passing the desired sub-song in `A`.
4) Repeatedly call `playAddress` (or let the player’s ISR drive it) at the cadence implied by `speed`.
5) Select sub-songs via re-invoking `init` with accumulator set to song number.

## Overview

This document captures the successful approach for creating pleasant, musical SID sounds on the Commodore 64, discovered through iterative testing with the MCP server and real hardware feedback.

records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sid-programming-best-practices.md#1. Ultra-Low Frequencies -->
### 1. Ultra-Low Frequencies

- **Critical Discovery**: The standard frequency tables from documentation are too high for pleasant listening
- **Working Range**: Use frequencies around 30-60 for the low byte, 0 for high byte
- **Result**: Produces warm, bass-like tones instead of harsh, screechy sounds

records.name: data/sound/sid-programming-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sid-programming-best-practices.md#2. Triangle Wave Instead of Pulse -->
### 2. Triangle Wave Instead of Pulse

- **Register 54276**: Use value `17` (triangle wave + GATE) instead of `33` (pulse wave + GATE)
- **Benefit**: Triangle waves are much smoother and more musical than pulse waves
- **Off State**: Use `16` (triangle wave, no GATE) to properly release notes

records.name: data/sound/sid-programming-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sid-programming-best-practices.md#4. Timing is Everything -->
### 4. Timing is Everything

- **Note Duration**: 3000 cycles provides proper sustain (~1.5 seconds)
- **Pause Duration**: 500 cycles between notes for clear separation
- **GATE Control**: Keep GATE on during entire note, then turn off cleanly

records.name: data/sound/sid-programming-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sid-programming-best-practices.md#5. Musical Expression and Phrasing -->
### 5. Musical Expression and Phrasing

- **Varied Note Lengths**: Don't make all notes the same duration - create rhythm and emphasis
- **Phrase Breathing**: Use longer pauses between musical phrases (150-200 cycles)
- **Dynamic Emphasis**: Emphasize important notes (phrase beginnings/endings) with longer durations
- **Narrative Flow**: Each phrase should have its own character and emotional arc
- **Quick Passages**: Use shorter notes (140-180 cycles) for rapid, flowing sections
- **Sustained Endings**: Use longer notes (400-600 cycles) for phrase climaxes and endings

## Musical Expression Example: "Alle meine Entchen"

The following example demonstrates how to create a musically expressive children's song using varied timing and proper phrasing. This serves as a template for writing engaging melodies.

records.name: data/sound/sid-programming-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sid-programming-best-practices.md#Key Musical Programming Principles -->
### Key Musical Programming Principles

1. **Opening Emphasis**: First note gets longer duration (250 cycles) to establish the song
2. **Flowing Middle**: Quick notes (180 cycles) for melodic flow
3. **Phrase Endings**: Extended notes (400-600 cycles) at the end of each phrase
4. **Breathing Space**: Longer pauses (150-200 cycles) between phrases
5. **Character Variation**: Each verse has its own timing character:
   - "Swimming" = light, quick notes (160 cycles)
   - "Diving" = very short, rapid notes (140 cycles)
   - "Triumphant ending" = building emphasis

records.name: data/sound/sid-programming-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sid-programming-best-practices.md#Timing Patterns for Different Musical Effects -->
### Timing Patterns for Different Musical Effects

- **Emphasis/Importance**: 250-400+ cycles
- **Normal melody notes**: 180-200 cycles  
- **Quick/flowing passages**: 140-160 cycles
- **Short pauses**: 25-40 cycles
- **Phrase breathing**: 120-200 cycles
- **Dramatic pauses**: 150-250 cycles

records.name: data/sound/sid-programming-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sid-programming-best-practices.md#Conclusion -->
## Conclusion

The key insight is that **musical programming requires human feedback**, not just technical accuracy. The "correct" mathematical frequencies from documentation don't necessarily produce the most pleasant musical experience. This approach prioritizes:

1. **Listenability** over technical accuracy
2. **Smooth waveforms** (triangle) over complex ones (pulse)
3. **Proper envelopes** for musical note shaping
4. **Musical expression** through varied timing and phrasing
5. **Real hardware testing** to validate results

**For Children's Songs and Simple Melodies**: Use the expressive timing patterns demonstrated in "Alle meine Entchen" to create engaging, musical compositions that tell a story rather than just playing notes mechanically.

This methodology can be applied to create more complex musical compositions while maintaining the warm, pleasant character achieved in this scale progression.

---

*Based on successful MCP server + C64 Ultimate testing session*

# Commodore 64 SID (MOS 6581 / 8580) — Concise Technical Overview

records.name: data/sound/sid-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sid-spec.md#Overview -->
## Overview

- **Voices:** 3 independent oscillators  
  Each has: 16-bit frequency, waveform select (triangle / saw / pulse / noise), pulse-width, ADSR envelope, optional SYNC and RING-MOD.  
- **Global:** Analog multimode filter (LP / BP / HP), resonance, master volume, and read-back registers for OSC3 and ENV3.  
- **Models:** 6581 (original, “warmer”, nonlinear filter) and 8580 (revised, linear filter, lower noise).

---

records.name: data/sound/sid-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sid-spec.md#Note → SID Frequency -->
## Note → SID Frequency

```
FREQ = round( note_hz * 2^24 / φ2 ) >> 8   ; 16-bit register value
```

- φ₂ = system clock  
  - PAL = 985 248 Hz  
  - NTSC = 1 022 727 Hz  
- Store FREQ (low/high) into FREQLO/HI.  
- Typical usage: lookup table per note/octave.

**Example (PAL):**

```
FREQ16 = round( (note_hz * 16777216) / 985248 ) >> 8
```

---

records.name: data/sound/sid-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sid-spec.md#Basic Play / Stop Sequence -->
## Basic Play / Stop Sequence

1. Set FREQ, PW, AD/SR.  
2. Write CTRL = waveform bits | GATE (=1) → start note.  
3. Clear GATE bit to release note.

---

records.name: data/sound/sid-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sid-spec.md#Waveforms & Pulse Width -->
## Waveforms & Pulse Width

- **Waveform bits:** Triangle = bit 4, Saw = 5, Pulse = 6, Noise = 7.  
- **Pulse Width:** 12-bit ($000–$FFF); $0800 ≈ 50 % duty.  
- Combining waveform bits produces nonlinear mixed timbres.  
- PWM = vary pulse-width in real time.

---

records.name: data/sound/sid-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sid-spec.md#Reset Tips -->
## Reset Tips

Write $FF then $00 to all SID registers on init to clear stale state before loading new instrument settings.

---

records.name: data/sound/sid-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sid-spec.md#Alternative Exact Frequency Formulas -->
## Alternative Exact Frequency Formulas

```
PAL:  x = f * (18 * 2^24) / 17734475
NTSC: x = f * (14 * 2^24) / 14318182
```

Equivalent to `FREQ = f * 2^24 / φ2`, then take the upper 16 bits.

records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sidwave.md#Patterns -->
## Patterns

Every pattern is a list of **entries**. Each entry lasts `length` beats (default 1; fractions allowed, e.g. `0.25` for sixteenth notes). The pattern repeats until its section ends; a note that would run past the section end is cut there.

- **groove** — `groove: [C2, "-", C2, "~", G1]`: one note per entry. `-` (or `.`) is a rest, `~` ties the entry to the previous note (no retrigger). A tie holds whatever note is sounding right before it, also across a section boundary (a section that starts with `~` continues the last note of the previous section). After a rest, or at the very start of the song, a tie is a rest.
- **arpeggio** — `type: arpeggio`, `notes: [...]`. Without `frame_rate`, the notes are played one per entry (a broken chord). With `frame_rate: N`, all notes form one entry that sounds as a fast chord arpeggio, switching to the next chord tone every N frames (`frame_rate: 1` = one tone per frame, about 50 per second on PAL); each entry retriggers the chord.
- **motif** — `motif: "..."` with tokens separated by spaces or commas:
  - note names (`C4`, `Eb3`, `F#2`),
  - integers: semitones above `root` (default `C3`), e.g. `"0 4 7 12"`,
  - chord symbols, expanded to their chord tones in the octave of `root`: `C`, `Cm`/`Cmin`, `Cdim`, `Caug`, `Csus2`, `Csus4`, `C6`, `Cm6`, `C7`, `Cmaj7`, `Cm7`, `Cdim7`, `Cm7b5`, `C9`, `Cmaj9`, `Cm9`/`Cmin9`, `Cadd9`,
  - `-` rests and `~` ties.
  Words that are not notes or chord symbols (such as `pad` or `motif`) are ignored. `"Cmin9 pad motif"` therefore plays C3, Eb3, G3, Bb3, D4, one per entry.

`transpositions: [0, 5, 7]` transposes successive repetitions of the pattern within a section by the given semitones, cycling; the cycle restarts at each section.

Notes range from C0 to B7. At the PAL clock B7 exceeds the SID's 16-bit frequency register, so the highest PAL note is A#7. Notes that leave the range after transposition are rejected.

records.name: data/sound/sidwave.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sidwave.md#Pattern effects (`fx`) -->
### Pattern effects (`fx`)

| Effect | Fields | Behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `vibrato` | `depth` (semitones, 0.03–6), `rate` (Hz, 0.2–12), `delay` (frames, optional) | Triangle pitch modulation of ±`depth` semitones around the note (the upward and downward swings are computed separately, so both reach `depth` to within the SID's frequency resolution, about 3 cents in the lowest octave), starting `delay` frames after the note. The upward swing must stay within the SID's highest frequency: on PAL a vibrato on A#7 can be at most 0.54 semitones deep, on NTSC B7 at most 0.19; deeper vibratos on such notes (including the highest note of a chord arpeggio) are rejected. The player samples the vibrato once per frame, so rates are limited to 12 Hz (about a quarter of the frame rate); faster rates would alias or cancel out. |
| `pwm_sweep` | `depth` (fraction ≤ 1 or 12-bit units), `speed` (cycles per second) | Pulse width moves linearly between `pulse_width − depth` and `pulse_width + depth`, restarting at the base on each note. Pulse waveform only. |
| `slide` | `depth` (semitones, ±24, non-zero), `speed` (frames, 1–255) | Each note starts `depth` semitones below the target (above when negative) and glides to it linearly in frequency, arriving after `speed` frames. The start note must itself be playable (C0..A#7 on PAL, C0..B7 on NTSC); otherwise the document is rejected. |
| `filter_mod` | `sweep: "+500 over 8 steps"` (units: `steps`, `beats`, `bars`, `frames`; a step is one entry), or `{ sweep: 500, beats: 8 }` | Routes the voice through the filter while the pattern plays. At each repetition of the pattern the cutoff offset restarts at 0 and ramps to `sweep` (cutoff units, −2047..2047) over the given time, then holds. The resulting cutoff is clamped to 0..2047. The offset is removed when the section ends. |

records.name: data/sound/sidwave.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sidwave.md#Timeline -->
## Timeline

Each section has `bars` (whole number ≥ 1), an optional `section` name, and `layers` mapping `v1`/`v2`/`v3` to a pattern reference:

- `"-"`, `.`, `rest` or an omitted layer: the voice is silent.
- `A`: play pattern `A` of that voice.
- Modifiers after the name: `↑` (or `^`) one octave up, `↓` one octave down, `+N` / `-N` N semitones (e.g. `A+5`), and a trailing `–`, `—` or `-` fades the voice out over the section.

Fading lowers the voice's sustain level linearly to 0 across the section. When every sounding voice of a section fades, the master volume also fades to 0 and returns to full volume when the section ends.

records.name: data/sound/sidwave.md
records.text:

### Not supported

Time signatures other than 4/4, per-note velocity, portamento between consecutive notes (the `slide` effect is a slide into each note), multiple subtunes, multispeed (more than one player call per frame), and combined waveforms.

## Configuration

Category "C64 and Cartridge Settings" (set with `c64_config`; changing it re-initialises the cartridge, a reset follows):

| Item | Values | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `RAM Expansion Unit` | Disabled, Enabled, GeoRAM Mode (mutually exclusive with REU) | Disabled |
| `REU Size` | 128 KB, 256 KB, 512 KB, 1 MB, 2 MB, 4 MB, 8 MB, 16 MB | 2 MB |
| `REU Preload` | Disabled, Enabled | Disabled |
| `REU Preload Image` | path, max 31 characters | `/Usb0/preload.reu` |
| `REU Preload Offset` | 0 KB, 128 KB ... 16 MB | 0 KB |

- An active REU disables cartridges that use `$DF00-$DFFF` (EasyFlash, Final Cartridge III).
- Reads beyond the configured size wrap and return plausible wrong data. Check the size at startup; a program should refuse to start with a text message naming the setting if the REU is missing or too small.
- REU contents survive C64 reset, `machine:reset` and `run_prg`; assume they are lost at power off.

## Detection

- `$DF1D & $7F = $49`: UCI on. Anything else: absent or off (a real REU returns `$FF`). Tell the user to enable `Command Interface`.
- Then IDENTIFY (`<target> 01`) once per target used; `NO TARGET` = absent.

records.name: data/ultimate/uci.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/ultimate/uci.md#Status strings -->
## Status strings

| Form | Used by | Success |
|---|---|---|
| `NN,TEXT` | DOS, Network, Control | `00,OK`; some commands return no status bytes |
| `NNN TEXT` | HTTP target errors | `000 OK`; after exchange: server response line plus headers (<=255 bytes) |
| 1 binary byte | SoftwareIEC | `$00` |
| bare text (`DISK IS FULL`, `WRITE PROTECTED`, ...) | DOS filesystem failures | non-digit first char = failure |

Codes mean different things per target, so key on target plus code. Common: `01` dir empty / connection closed by host, `02` request truncated / no data, `04` datagram truncated, `11` connect error, `12` send/close error, `21` UNKNOWN COMMAND, `81` INVALID PARAMS, `82` DOS file not found, `83` DOS no such directory / net interface not available, `84` DOS no file to close / net unresolved host / control REU not enabled, `85` DOS no file open / net socket error, `88`/`89` config file cannot open / had errors (control), `89` not a disk image (DOS), `90` drive not present, `98` prohibited.

records.text:
<!-- Source: data/ultimate/uci.md#Target 6: HTTP (firmware 3.15, 2026-05) -->
## Target 6: HTTP (firmware 3.15, 2026-05)

Header and body objects live in the Ultimate (16 slots each, machine-wide; a crashed program leaks them: FREE_ALL at startup). One exchange takes seconds to tens of seconds (DNS, connect, transfer). HTTPS works (certificate validation unverified). No ranges: a reply larger than your buffer is truncated.

| Cmd | Name | Args | Reply |
|---|---|---|---|
| 01 | IDENTIFY | - | `ULTIMATE HTTP TARGET V1.0` |
| 10 | FREE_ALL | - | |
| 11 / 12 | HEADER_CREATE / FREE | `<verb> <url>` / `<h>` | header handle; verbs GET 01 PUT 02 POST 03 PATCH 04 DELETE 05 HEAD 06 OPTIONS 07 |
| 13 / 14 / 15 | HEADER_ADD / QUERY / LIST | `<h> "Key: value"` / `<h> <key>` / `<h> <index>` | |
| 21 / 22 | BODY_CREATE / FREE | `<fmt>` / `<h>` | formats: BINARY 01, JSON OBJECT 02, JSON ARRAY 03, URL ENCODED 04 |
| 23-27 | BODY_ADD_INT/BOOL/STRING/OBJECT/ARRAY | `<h> <keylen> <key> <value>` | |
| 2A | BODY_QUERY | `<h> <path>` | typed value; the Ultimate parses JSON, the C64 needs no parser |
| 2C-2E | BODY_ADD_BINARY / ADD / CLEAR | | binary: repeat to append |
| 31 | DO_EXCHANGE_OBJ | `<hdr> <body or FF>` | response header and body handles |
| 32 | DO_EXCHANGE_RAW | `<hdr> <body or FF>` | response body bytes in blocks; status = server response line plus headers |

HTTP errors: `400` bad command/index, `404` key/entry not found, `500` bad format, `503` service unavailable, `507` no free slot. Minimal GET: `06 11 01 <url>` then `06 32 <hdr> FF`, read body blocks, `06 12 <hdr>`. URL `http://host[:port]/path`; Content-Type/Length are added automatically for bodies.

## Game use

- Levels: DOS open/seek/read 512-byte blocks (pack levels in one indexed file), SoftwareIEC LOAD for whole PRGs, or LOAD_REU once then DMA per level (c64://ultimate/reu).
- High scores: open `$0E`, WRITE_DATA, CLOSE; read back with `$01`; FILE_STAT checks existence/size. Handle `DISK IS FULL`/`WRITE PROTECTED`. Do not use `/Temp` for persistence.
- Settings: write `.cfg`, LOAD_CONFIG. Network play: TCP/UDP relay or HTTP JSON; never block in the frame loop.

records.name: data/vice/vice-binary-monitor-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/vice/vice-binary-monitor-spec.md#Core Protocol Rules -->
## Core Protocol Rules

- The VICE binary monitor uses a dedicated connection configured with `-binarymonitor` and `-binarymonitoraddress`.
- Every packet starts with `STX = 0x02`.
- There is no packet terminator.
- Packet boundaries are determined by the length field in the frame header.
- Current API version: `0x02`.
- All multibyte integers are little-endian.
- Boolean fields use `0x00 = false`, `>= 0x01 = true`.
- Direct responses echo the command `request_id`.
- Responses with `request_id = 0xffffffff` are asynchronous events.
- Commands may cause asynchronous monitor-entry events before the direct command response.
- Register IDs and bank IDs are machine-dependent. Do not hard-code them.
- Use `REGISTERS_AVAILABLE` and `BANKS_AVAILABLE` to resolve IDs.
- Many array items include an item-size field. Use it to skip future extensions.

---

## Notation

| Notation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `u8` | 1 byte unsigned |
| `u16` | 2 byte unsigned, little-endian |
| `u32` | 4 byte unsigned, little-endian |
| `u64` | 8 byte unsigned, little-endian |
| `bytes[N]` | exactly `N` bytes |
| `str[N]` | `N` bytes, not null-terminated unless stated otherwise |
| `FIELD?` | optional field |
| `ITEM[N]` | `N` repeated items |

---

records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/agent-state-spec.md#c64bridge — Agent State Specification -->
# c64bridge — Agent State Specification

This specification defines how the **c64bridge** agent stores and manages its persistent **task** and **session** state.

A **task** is the fundamental unit of work executed by the agent. There are two task types:

- **Foreground tasks** — short-lived, single-execution operations (e.g., extract sprites from RAM).  
- **Background tasks** — long-running, periodic operations (e.g., sample memory every second).

---

records.name: doc/agent-state-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/agent-state-spec.md#1. Directory Layout -->
## 1. Directory Layout

All state is stored under the user’s home directory (`~/.c64bridge/`).

```text
~/.c64bridge/
 ├─ tasks.json                  # global registry of all tasks (foreground + background)
 └─ tasks/
     ├─ background/             # background (recurring) tasks
   │   └─ <taskId>/           # e.g. 0001_read
     │       ├─ task.json
     │       ├─ result.json
     │       └─ log.txt
     └─ <taskId>/               # foreground (one-shot) tasks
         ├─ task.json
         ├─ result.json
         ├─ artifacts/          # optional outputs (e.g., sprites, dumps)
         └─ log.txt
```

records.name: doc/agent-state-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/agent-state-spec.md#2. Task Types -->
## 2. Task Types

records.name: doc/agent-state-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/agent-state-spec.md#Background Tasks -->
### Background Tasks

- Long-running, recurring operations that execute periodically.  
- Used for sampling, monitoring, or repeated execution of a fixed operation.

Examples:

- Read C64 memory every second for 1 minute.  
- Poll the C64 screen until specific text appears.  
- Periodically capture state for regression detection.

Background tasks have an interval and optional maximum iteration count.

---

records.name: doc/agent-state-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/agent-state-spec.md#6. session.json — Session Summary (optional) -->
## 6. session.json — Session Summary (optional)

Sessions are logical groupings of tasks run in the same time window.  
This file is optional and only created if session tracking is enabled.

```json
{
  "sessionId": "2025-10-27T11-42-00Z",
  "created": "2025-10-27T11-42-00Z",
  "ended": null,
  "status": "active",
  "tasks": [
    { "id": "0001_extract_sprites", "type": "foreground" },
    { "id": "0002_read", "type": "background" }
  ]
}
```

---

records.name: doc/agent-state-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/agent-state-spec.md#7. Update & Persistence Model -->
## 7. Update & Persistence Model

- **In-memory source of truth:** `TASKS: Map<string, Task>`
- **On-disk persistence:** `~/.c64bridge/tasks.json`
- On startup:
  - `ensureTasksLoaded()` loads `tasks.json`.
  - If missing, an empty file is created.
- On every task state change:
  - Update `tasks.json` (atomic rewrite).
  - Write or update the per-task `task.json` and optional `result.json`.
- **Timestamps:** All stored as UTC strings in `YYYY-MM-DDTHH-mm-ssZ` format.

---

records.name: doc/audit/secret-handling.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/audit/secret-handling.md#Ultimate network password handling audit -->
# Ultimate network password handling audit

**Summary: yes, a leak exists.** An Ultimate request failure can leave the password in an Axios error's request configuration, which reaches stderr when a screen read fails during BASIC execution or polling. This is a source audit, supplemented by a local synthetic Axios serialization/console check; it does not establish that a real password was exposed. Diagnostics usually reduce actual `Error` objects to selected fields, and ordinary MCP error conversion usually uses only the message, but neither is a general secret boundary. Firmware-returned data and arbitrary error messages are not redacted.

records.name: doc/audit/secret-handling.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/audit/secret-handling.md#Paths checked -->
- **General logger and console — leak.** `src/logger.ts:37`–`47` passes details to console unchanged; `src/bootstrap/stdio-logger.ts:25`–`33` directs console output to stderr. `C64Client.readScreen` calls `readMemoryRaw` (`src/c64Client.ts:900`–`904`), which rethrows a non-unsupported facade error (`:2169`–`:2177`). After BASIC upload, `src/tools/programRunners.ts:381`–`385` logs that raw error as details (`:34`–`:41`); Node console inspection prints Axios `config.headers`, including the password. With debug logging enabled, `src/tools/pollValidator.ts:169`–`170` and `:192`–`:193` likewise log the raw error (also `:255`–`:256`, `:279`–`:280`). Other console sites were inspected by search: startup connectivity logs a message rather than the Axios object (`src/mcp-server.ts:650`–`660`), while fatal logging prints an arbitrary raw error (`:738`–`:745`), so it has the same unsafe sink if such an error reaches it. `src/config.ts:62`–`69` prints JSON parser error messages; malformed configuration can put a fragment of the file in that message, so this is another potential credential disclosure, dependent on the malformed input and Node version.

records.name: doc/audit/secret-handling.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/audit/secret-handling.md#Paths checked -->
- **Diagnostic event files — safe for ordinary Axios Error configuration; otherwise unclear.** `writeDiagnosticEvent` calls `sanitize` before appending NDJSON (`src/diagnostics.ts:112`–`128`); actual `Error` instances are reduced to name, message, stack, code and sanitized cause, omitting Axios config (`:444`–`:453`). This applies to the raw connectivity error (`src/mcp-server.ts:650`–`659`), span failures (`src/diagnostics.ts:198`–`211`), MCP failure events (`src/mcp-server.ts:395`–`415`), and process handlers (`src/diagnostics.ts:410`–`422`). However, plain objects are traversed without key redaction (`:483`–`:488`), and strings, messages and stacks are retained (`:445`–`:456`); call-tool arguments are recorded (`src/mcp-server.ts:350`–`357`). Thus a serialized error, echoed credential, or user-supplied password can be persisted; no automatic flow from the configured header into those plain-object events was established. Diagnostics are enabled by default outside tests unless explicitly disabled (`src/diagnostics.ts:434`–`441`).

records.name: doc/audit/secret-handling.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/audit/secret-handling.md#Paths checked -->
- **MCP results and errors — safe for ordinary Axios config; unclear for returned firmware data.** `C64Client.normaliseError` selects message, status and response data for Axios errors (`src/c64Client.ts:2426`–`2439`); for example `readMemory` returns those details (`:927`–`:949`). `unknownErrorResult` uses an Error's message rather than serializing the Error (`src/tools/errors.ts:104`–`121`), while `toolErrorResult` includes supplied details (`:78`–`:93`) and `toCallToolResult` passes result fields through (`src/mcp-server.ts:690`–`713`). `version`, `info` and `configGet` can propagate raw Axios errors (`src/device.ts:357`–`358`, `:418`–`:422`; `src/c64Client.ts:1145`–`1152`, `:1416`–`:1423`), but their ordinary tool catches use the message. No direct serialization of one of these raw Axios errors into a client result was established. Response data is unfiltered, however: `config_get` returns firmware values (`src/tools/developer.ts:219`–`237`); whether firmware exposes its password there or echoes it on error is not established. User-supplied config values can also be returned (`:255`–`:280`).

- **MCP resources and diagnostic reports — unclear for indirect content.** Platform status constructs backend and capability text, not endpoint credentials (`src/mcp-server.ts:197`–`219`, `:543`–`:604`); resource failures log messages, record sanitized errors and rethrow (`:236`–`:249`). `performance_report` reads diagnostic records and returns a summary (`src/tools/meta/diagnostics.ts:75`–`99`; `src/diagnostics.ts:235`–`249`, `:256` onward), so any sensitive content retained in the diagnostic timeline may reach a client. No direct configured-header-to-resource leak was established.

records.name: doc/audit/secret-handling.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/audit/secret-handling.md#Paths checked -->
- **Thrown and rethrown errors — leak across internal error boundary.** The original Axios error is rethrown by `readMemoryRaw` (`src/c64Client.ts:2169`–`2177`), by `withDiagnosticSpan` (`src/diagnostics.ts:198`–`211`), and by stream retry and capture paths (`src/c64Client.ts:1963`–`1971`, `:1978`–`:1983`, `:1633`–`:1638`, `:1883`–`:1895`). It still contains the request config; `JSON.stringify` invokes Axios's `toJSON` and exposes the header without opt-in redaction. `ensureStreamSuccess` embeds serialized result details in a new error (`:2023`–`:2027`), but no proven route from a raw Axios config into those details was found. Raw errors reaching generic console sinks remain a concrete risk.

- **Other files — unclear for firmware-returned secrets.** Config snapshot collection stores returned values (`src/tools/meta/configInventory.ts:86`–`101`) and snapshot writes them to a file (`src/tools/meta/config.ts:40`–`54`). Whether the firmware returns the network password is unverified; the bridge does not insert its configured header value into the snapshot itself.

records.name: doc/audit/secret-handling.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/audit/secret-handling.md#Recommended fixes -->
## Recommended fixes

1. In `createLoggingHttpClient`, replace or sanitize rejected Axios errors before they leave the transport, removing sensitive headers from config and request objects; apply the same boundary to direct Axios calls in `logConnectivity` and `C64uBackend.ping`. Preserve useful status and message fields without retaining credential-bearing causes.
2. In `createPrefixedLogger` and the error logging in `pollBasicOutcome`, the ASM polling function, and BASIC program execution, log safe error summaries rather than raw objects; in `loadConfig`, avoid printing parser excerpts from configuration files. Review the fatal `main().catch` console sink as well.
3. In `sanitize` and `writeDiagnosticEvent`, redact sensitive keys recursively and handle serialized Axios errors, arguments and error strings deliberately. In `normaliseError`, `unknownErrorResult`, `toolErrorResult`, and `toCallToolResult`, enforce a safe output boundary for errors and echoed data.
4. In `config_get`'s `execute` and `captureConfigSnapshot`, decide how sensitive firmware configuration values should be handled and redact them if returned. Add focused tests with a synthetic password covering stderr, diagnostics, serialized errors, tool responses and snapshots.

records.name: doc/audit/secret-handling.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/audit/secret-handling.md#Outcome of the fix -->
## Outcome of the fix

The audit findings above describe the code before this change. This change adds one shared helper, `src/redact.ts`, and applies it at each sink.

- `registerSecret` records the password. It is called from `resolveUltimateEndpoint` (`src/config.ts`), from `createLoggingHttpClient` (which reads the `X-Password` header it is configured with), and before the direct connectivity probe in `src/mcp-server.ts`.
- `scrubRequestError` is applied to every rejected request in `createLoggingHttpClient`. It replaces sensitive values in `error.config.headers` and `error.response.config.headers`, clears `error.request` and `error.response.request` (the raw client request keeps the serialised header block), and redacts the password in a string response body. The status, code, message and response data otherwise remain available to callers. This closes the "thrown and rethrown errors" and `JSON.stringify` leaks.
- `redactValue` and `redactText` are applied in `createPrefixedLogger` (`src/logger.ts`) to the message and details, in `sanitize` (`src/diagnostics.ts`) before the existing size limiting, in `toCallToolResult` (`src/mcp-server.ts`) to `content`, `structuredContent` and `metadata`, and to the fatal error in `main().catch`. `redactValue` reduces `Error` objects to name, message, stack, code, status and cause, redacts credential header names at any depth, and replaces registered secrets in all strings.
- `loadConfig` now logs only the error name for an unreadable configuration file, because the JSON parser message can quote part of the file.

records.name: doc/audit/secret-handling.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/audit/secret-handling.md#Outcome of the fix -->
Remaining limitation: redaction replaces the exact registered password string. A transformed form of the password (for example base64-encoded) is not detected. Firmware configuration values are handled separately, see below.

Regression test: `test/secretRedaction.test.mjs` configures a distinctive password through `C64U_PASSWORD`, then drives HTTP 401 (with the password echoed in the body), HTTP 403, a client timeout and a refused connection against local servers. It asserts that the password is absent from captured console output, diagnostics files and records, `util.inspect`, `JSON.stringify`, `toJSON` and `stack` of the errors, and from `toCallToolResult` output for `toolErrorResult` and `unknownErrorResult`. With `src/redact.ts` replaced by no-op functions and the other `src/` changes reverted, the test fails with "password leaked in: AxiosError: Request failed with status code 401". With the fix it passes. `npm test` passes.

records.name: doc/audit/secret-handling.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/audit/secret-handling.md#Firmware-returned configuration values -->
- Opt-in: `includeSecretValues: true` on `config_get` and on `config_snapshot_and_restore` returns or stores the values in plain text. Without the flag the values are never returned or written. The configured network password is still replaced by the registered-secret redaction in `toCallToolResult`, even with the flag.
- Restore: a default snapshot contains `***`. `stripRedactedSecrets` removes those placeholders from the restore payload, so a restore never sets a password to the literal `***`. Credentials in a default snapshot are therefore not restored. Snapshots made with `includeSecretValues: true` restore them.
- Diff: both sides are redacted by default, so a changed password is not reported unless the flag is set when the snapshot is taken and when diffing.
- Limitation: detection is by item name. A credential item with a name that does not match the patterns above is not redacted.

**Test.** `test/configSecretRedaction.test.mjs` uses a mocked firmware with "Network Password", "FTP Password", "Telnet Password" and a Wi-Fi "Password". It asserts redaction in the `config_get` result and in the written snapshot file, that other values (Hostname, Volume, access point name) are unchanged, that restore does not write `***`, and that the opt-in flag returns plain values. With `isSensitiveConfigItem` changed to always return false, 3 of its 4 tests fail.

# C64 REST API Reference

This document is a concise version of the official [Ultimate REST API guide](https://1541u-documentation.readthedocs.io/en/latest/api/api_calls.html).

records.name: doc/c64u/c64-rest-api.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/c64u/c64-rest-api.md#HTTP Basics -->
## HTTP Basics

- REST access starts from Ultimate firmware 3.11.
- URLs follow the form `/v1/{route}/{path}:{command}?{arguments}`.

| Verb | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| GET | Retrieves information without changing state. |
| PUT | Sends information or performs an action using the information in the URL or in a referenced file. |
| POST | Performs an action using information attached to the request. |

- Responses normally use `Content-Type: application/json` and always include an `errors` array.
- Firmware 3.12 introduces the optional Network Password. When it is set, include `X-Password: {your-password}` in every request. The firmware returns `403 Forbidden` when the header is missing or incorrect. Supplying the header on an unsecured unit is accepted and ignored.

records.text:

## Routes

The sections below follow the order and wording of the RST reference.

### Data Streams (Ultimate 64)

| Method | Path | Parameters | Action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PUT | `/v1/streams/{stream}:start` | `ip` | Starts the selected stream (`video`, `audio`, or `debug`). Supply an IP address and optional port (defaults: `video` 11000, `audio` 11001, `debug` 11002). Starting the video stream stops the debug stream. |
| PUT | `/v1/streams/{stream}:stop` | – | Stops the selected stream (`video`, `audio`, or `debug`). |

records.name: doc/c64u/c64-rest-api.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/c64u/c64-rest-api.md#File Manipulation -->
### File Manipulation

| Method | Path | Parameters | Action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GET | `/v1/files/{path}:info` | – | Returns file information such as size and extension. Supports wildcards. Marked unfinished in firmware 3.11 alpha. |
| PUT | `/v1/files/{path}:create_d64` | `[tracks]`, `[diskname]` | Creates a D64 image. Tracks default to 35 and may be set to 40. An optional disk name overrides the header title. |
| PUT | `/v1/files/{path}:create_d71` | `[diskname]` | Creates a D71 image with 70 tracks. An optional disk name overrides the header title. |
| PUT | `/v1/files/{path}:create_d81` | `[diskname]` | Creates a D81 image with 160 tracks. An optional disk name overrides the header title. |
| PUT | `/v1/files/{path}:create_dnp` | `tracks`, `[diskname]` | Creates a DNP image. Tracks are required (maximum 255, 256 sectors per track). An optional disk name overrides the header title. |

## 9. Troubleshooting Cheatsheet

- Missing entrypoint? Ensure dev deps are installed or run `./build build` so [`dist/index.js`](../dist/index.js) exists.
- Tool not exposed? Confirm registry wiring (`src/tools/registry/index.ts`) and rebuild.
- Real-device tests flaky? Verify `C64_TEST_BASE_URL` reachability; replay curl probes while the HTTP bridge is active.
- Empty RAG answers? Rebuild embeddings (`./build rag:rebuild`) and confirm `RAG_EMBEDDINGS_DIR` points at committed data.
- Logs quiet? Remember all server logs emit to stderr to keep stdout dedicated to MCP.

Stay in lockstep with the [README](../README.md) and [`AGENTS.md`](../AGENTS.md) when introducing features so external docs remain accurate.

## Persistent Diagnostics

The MCP server now writes a newline-delimited JSON diagnostics file for each session.

- Default location: `~/.c64bridge/diagnostics/`
- Override location: set `C64BRIDGE_DIAGNOSTICS_DIR=/path/to/dir`
- Disable only if necessary: set `C64BRIDGE_DISABLE_DIAGNOSTICS=1`

Each file records:

- MCP startup and readiness
- tool, prompt, and resource request lifecycle events
- unhandled rejections, warnings, and uncaught exceptions
- VICE/Xvfb startup failures with captured stderr and stdout tails

When VS Code or Copilot appears to crash, preserve the newest `.ndjson` file before restarting. It is the fastest way to tell whether the MCP server was failing, hanging, or repeatedly restarting.

## Common Issues & Fixes

<!-- Source: doc/troubleshooting-mcp.md#1. Server Starts Without Connectivity Logs -->
### 1. Server Starts Without Connectivity Logs

**Symptoms:**

- `npm start` prints the banner but omits `Connectivity check succeeded`.
- CI job `Validate MCP server logs` fails.

**Resolution:**

1. Confirm the REST base URL in `.c64bridge.json` or `C64BRIDGE_CONFIG` matches a reachable device.
2. Run `curl -I http://<host>/v1/info` to confirm HTTP reachability.
3. Review `src/mcp-server.ts` connectivity logging; ensure no local edits suppressed `logConnectivity`.
4. If hardware is offline, expect `Skipping direct REST connectivity probe` in the logs—CI treats this as success.
records.origin: doc/troubleshooting-mcp.md#1. Server Starts Without Connectivity Logs

records.name: doc/troubleshooting-mcp.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/troubleshooting-mcp.md#2. VS Code (Copilot Chat) Cannot See Tools -->
### 2. VS Code (Copilot Chat) Cannot See Tools

**Symptoms:**

- Copilot Chat shows "No MCP server" messages.
- Tool invocations fail silently.

**Resolution:**

1. Restart VS Code after changing MCP settings.
2. Verify the settings JSON matches the snippet in `AGENTS.md` (`command`, `args`, `type: "stdio"`).
3. Keep `npm start` (or `npx c64bridge`) running; Copilot terminates the stdio process when the chat closes.
4. Inspect the Copilot output channel for connection errors and ensure the stdio server entry is configured and running.
5. Correlate the VS Code/Copilot timestamp with the newest file under `~/.c64bridge/diagnostics/`.

If the entire VS Code window crashes rather than just the MCP session, also collect:

- VS Code logs from `Help` -> `Open Logs Folder`
- extension host logs and crash dumps from the same time window
- the matching `.ndjson` file from `~/.c64bridge/diagnostics/`
records.origin: doc/troubleshooting-mcp.md#2. VS Code (Copilot Chat) Cannot See Tools

### 3. Tests Fail Because Mock Server Is Missing

**Symptoms:**

- `npm test` exits with ENOENT for `test/mockC64Server.mjs` or cannot bind to port 18064.

**Resolution:**

1. Ensure dev dependencies are installed (`npm install`).
2. Verify nothing else occupies the mock server port: `lsof -i :18064`.
3. Run `npm test -- --verbose` to see which suite fails; the harness spins up the mock server automatically.

## Key Lessons Learned

1. Connectivity logs are the fastest signal—watch the console during startup.
2. The diagnostics `.ndjson` file is now the authoritative crash trail for MCP sessions.
3. Keep configuration files small and explicit; mismatched hosts cause silent timeouts.
4. Automated tests cover most workflows; run `npm test` before suspecting hardware.

records.text:

## 2. Transport Format

records.name: doc/vice/vice-binary-monitor-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/vice/vice-binary-monitor-spec.md#2.1 Command Packet -->
### 2.1 Command Packet

| Offset | Size | Field | Description |
|---------|------|--------|-------------|
| 0 | 1 | `0x02` | Start-of-text (STX) |
| 1 | 1 | API version | Client API version (`0x01` or `0x02`) |
| 2–5 | 4 | Body length | Byte count of the command body |
| 6–9 | 4 | Request ID | Caller-specified identifier echoed in responses |
| 10 | 1 | Command ID | See §5 |
| 11+ | N | Command body | Command payload |

The current implementation accepts headers tagged with API version `0x01` or `0x02`. Commands introduced in API 0x02 (`Keyboard Feed`, `Display Get`) require clients to transmit `0x02`; otherwise the monitor returns error `0x82`.

records.name: doc/vice/vice-binary-monitor-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/vice/vice-binary-monitor-spec.md#2.2 Response Packet -->
### 2.2 Response Packet

| Offset | Size | Field | Description |
|---------|------|--------|-------------|
| 0 | 1 | `0x02` | Start-of-text (STX) |
| 1 | 1 | API version | Always `MON_BINARY_API_VERSION` (0x02) |
| 2–5 | 4 | Body length | Byte count of the response body |
| 6 | 1 | Response type | Usually the command ID |
| 7 | 1 | Error code | See §2.3 |
| 8–11 | 4 | Request ID | Mirrors the request; 0xffffffff for events |
| 12+ | N | Response body | Response payload (may be empty) |

records.name: doc/vice/vice-binary-monitor-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/vice/vice-binary-monitor-spec.md#2.3 Error Codes -->
### 2.3 Error Codes

| Code | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| 0x00 | Success |
| 0x01 | Object missing (e.g. unknown breakpoint or joystick port) |
| 0x02 | Invalid memspace |
| 0x80 | Command length mismatch |
| 0x81 | Invalid parameter |
| 0x82 | Unsupported API version |
| 0x83 | Unknown command |
| 0x8F | Command failed |

---

records.text:

## 3. Addressing and Metadata

| Value | Memspace |
|-------|----------|
| 0 | `e_comp_space` (main computer CPU) |
| 1 | `e_disk8_space` |
| 2 | `e_disk9_space` |
| 3 | `e_disk10_space` |
| 4 | `e_disk11_space` |
| other | invalid (`memspace_to_uint8_t` exports 0xff) |

Banks are 16-bit values. Use `0x82 Banks Available` to enumerate valid bank numbers for the main computer CPU; on memspaces without banks the monitor ignores the supplied bank value.

Register lists omit entries flagged with `MON_REGISTER_IS_FLAGS`. Register values are truncated to 16 bits in the binary protocol even if the underlying register is wider; the `size` metadata tells the real width in bits.

<!-- Source: doc/vice/vice-binary-monitor-spec.md#4. Asynchronous Messages -->
## 4. Asynchronous Messages

Responses sent with request ID `0xffffffff` are unsolicited events:

- Monitor open: emits `0x31 Register Info` (memspace `e_comp_space`) followed by `0x62 Stopped` with the current PC.
- Monitor close: emits `0x63 Resumed` with the current PC.
- Checkpoint hits: `mon_breakpoint.c` emits `0x11 Checkpoint Info` with `hit = 1`.
- CPU JAM: `0x61 Jam` is sent, currently with an empty body (the PC is not transmitted because the handler passes length 0).
- Other responses (e.g. `Checkpoint List`) reuse the same response types but keep the original request ID.

## 5. Command Reference

records.name: doc/vice/vice-binary-monitor-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/vice/vice-binary-monitor-spec.md#Register Access (0x31–0x32) -->
### Register Access (0x31–0x32)

#### 0x31 – Registers Get

- Request: `[0] memspace`
- Response (`0x31`): `[0–1] register count`, followed by entries `[size,id,value_lo,value_hi]`
- Notes: Only registers without `MON_REGISTER_IS_FLAGS` are returned. `size` is always 3 and values carry the low 16 bits of the hardware register.

#### 0x32 – Registers Set

- Request: `[0] memspace, [1–2] count, [3+] entries` where each entry begins `[size,id,value_lo,value_hi,…]`
- Response (`0x31`): refreshed register list for the same memspace
- Notes: The monitor validates each register with `mon_register_valid`. Only the first two value bytes are used; extra bytes (if any) are skipped.

records.name: doc/vice/vice-binary-monitor-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/vice/vice-binary-monitor-spec.md#Snapshots (0x41–0x42) -->
### Snapshots (0x41–0x42)

#### 0x41 – Dump Snapshot

- Request: `[0] save ROMs flag, [1] save disks flag, [2] file name length, [3+] path`
- Response (`0x41`): empty
- Notes: The monitor inserts a trailing NUL before calling `mon_write_snapshot`. Failure yields `0x8F`.

#### 0x42 – Undump Snapshot

- Request: `[0] file name length, [1+] path`
- Response (`0x42`): `[0–1] current PC`
- Notes: On success the monitor reloads the snapshot via `mon_read_snapshot`, updates the dot address, and reports the new program counter.

records.name: doc/vice/vice-binary-monitor-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/vice/vice-binary-monitor-spec.md#Resources (0x51–0x52) -->
### Resources (0x51–0x52)

#### 0x51 – Resource Get

- Request: `[0] name length, [1+] name`
- Response (`0x51`): string resources → `[0]=0, [1] value length, [2+] bytes`; integer resources → `[0]=1, [1]=4, [2–5] value`
- Notes: Name length must be ≥1 and ≤255; strings are limited to 255 bytes. Unknown resources return `0x01`.

#### 0x52 – Resource Set

- Request: `[0] value type (0=string,1=int), [1] name length, [2+] name, [N] value length, [N+] value`
- Response (`0x52`): empty
- Notes: Strings are NUL-terminated by the monitor before dispatch. Integer payloads may be 1, 2, or 4 bytes; other sizes trigger `0x80`. Type mismatches yield `0x81`.

records.name: doc/vice/vice-binary-monitor-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/vice/vice-binary-monitor-spec.md#Execution Control (0x71–0x73) -->
### Execution Control (0x71–0x73)

#### 0x71 – Advance Instructions

- Request: `[0] step-over flag, [1–2] instruction count`
- Response (`0x71`): empty
- Notes: When the flag is non-zero the monitor uses `mon_instructions_next`, otherwise `mon_instructions_step`.

#### 0x72 – Keyboard Feed

- Request: `[0] length, [1+] PETSCII text`
- Response (`0x72`): empty
- Notes: Requires command header API version `0x02`; otherwise the monitor returns `0x82`. The server appends a NUL before calling `kbdbuf_feed`.

#### 0x73 – Execute Until Return

- Request: empty
- Response (`0x73`): empty
- Notes: Invokes `mon_instruction_return()`.

records.name: doc/vice/vice-binary-monitor-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: doc/vice/vice-binary-monitor-spec.md#Palette and I/O (0x91–0xB2) -->
### Palette and I/O (0x91–0xB2)

#### 0x91 – Palette Get

- Request: `[0] use alternate canvas flag`
- Response (`0x91`): `[0–1] entry count, [2+] entries` where each entry is `[size, red, green, blue]`
- Notes: Shares the same canvas selection logic as `Display Get`. The `size` field is always 3.

#### 0xA2 – Joyport Set

- Request: `[0–1] port number, [2–3] value`
- Response (`0xA2`): empty
- Notes: Delegates to `mon_joyport_set_output`. Invalid port → `0x01`; illegal value → `0x81`; other failures → `0x8F`.

#### 0xB2 – Userport Set

- Request: `[0–1] value`
- Response (`0xB2`): empty
- Notes: Delegates to `mon_userport_set_output`. Illegal values return `0x81`; other errors return `0x8F`.

## 6. Response Types

| ID | Type | Description | Body |
|----|------|-------------|------|
| 0x00 | Invalid | Error container | usually empty |
| 0x11 | Checkpoint Info | Checkpoint state | `[0–3] number, [4] hit, [5–6] start, [7–8] end, [9] stop, [10] enabled, [11] op mask, [12] temporary, [13–16] hit count, [17–20] ignore count, [21] has condition, [22] memspace` |
| 0x31 | Register Info | Register snapshot | `[0–1] count` followed by entries `(size,id,value_lo,value_hi)` |
| 0x61 | Jam | CPU jammed | empty (PC is not transmitted in the current implementation) |
| 0x62 | Stopped | Execution halted | `[0–1] current PC` |
| 0x63 | Resumed | Execution resumed | `[0–1] current PC` |
